newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Yeltsin to visit Ukraine, sign friendship pact.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to visit Ukraine, sign friendship pact.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin starts his first state visit to Ukraine on Friday, described by the Kremlin as his main foreign policy step this year and by observers as the end of a "cold war" between Moscow and Kiev.
Yeltsin, who has postponed visiting Kiev six times, is due to sign a long-awaited bilateral friendship treaty with Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Saturday.
"(It is) the most difficult visit and the most important foreign policy act by the Russian President in 1997," Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.
Moscow and Kiev, which played crucial roles in ending the Soviet Union in late 1991, have since been caught in a web of mutual recriminations over the heritage of the communist empire.
Rows over the disputed Black Sea Fleet, Ukraine's energy debt and the fate of Soviet nuclear missiles have combined with other problems to sour bilateral relations.

"Yeltsin's visit to Kiev and massive talks held ahead of it herald a broad political agreement which is expected to take away the huge strains of the undeclared cold war between two former 'sister-republics'," the Ukraina Moloda daily wrote.
The draft friendship treaty has not been released, but Russia's Nezavisimaya Gazeta published parts of it on Friday.
"(Russia and Ukraine) respect each other's territorial integrity and confirm that the existing border between them cannot be changed," the treaty said without elaboration.

Russia's influential nationalists have insisted the Kremlin should question Ukraine's right to Crimea, the Russian-dominated Black Sea region handed over by the Soviet leadership in the 1950s from Russia to Ukraine. Both at that time were republics of the Soviet Union.
"Each side will not take part or support steps aimed at the other party and promises not to strike deals with third parties aimed at the other partner," one clause said.

Kuchma and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who met in Kiev on Wednesday, signed a series of deals they said had solved all bilateral problems ahead of the summit meeting, including the shareout of the Black Sea fleet.
Under the deal Russia won a 20-year lease of the naval base of Sevastopol in Urkaine's Crimean peninsula to keep its lion's share of the rusting Soviet-era force.
The decision stirred emotions among nationalists in Kiev, who according to the respected Den daily were planning to greet Yeltsin "like hooligans" with protests against his visit.
The Ukrainian opposition daily Den suggested that Moscow's new commitment to seal a friendship treaty with Kiev was part of the Kremlin's wider political game with NATO.
Yeltsin has signed a deal which gives Moscow some say in the Western alliance in exchange for an unspoken assent to NATO's plans to grant membership to some Eastern European countries.
But bowing to the inevitable admission to NATO of Moscow's Cold War allies in the Warsaw pact, the Kremlin stressed it would not tolerate former Soviet republics joining.
The three Baltic States of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania are seeking full membership of NATO and Moscow had feared Ukraine might follow suit.
On Thursday Ukraine tacitly accepted it would not seek NATO membership by initialling a separate security pact with the Western alliance in the Portugese town of Sintra.
